title: At home
description: Rooms and furniture, the accusative den, and describing your home with adjectives. Then view a flat for rent.

grammarNotes.title: Rooms and furniture: der, die or das?
grammarNotes.body:
Learn every noun with its article. There's no rule for most of them, but one trick helps a lot:

When a word is built from two parts, the **last part** decides the article. *Schlafzimmer* (schlafen + Zimmer) and *Wohnzimmer* (wohnen + Zimmer) are both **das**, because it's *das Zimmer*.

*Zimmer* and *Fenster* don't change in the plural: *ein Zimmer, zwei Zimmer*.

grammarNotes.title: The accusative: der becomes den
grammarNotes.body:
You met the accusative in *Food & drink*: when a noun is the **object** of a verb (the thing you need, want, have or look for), *ein* becomes *einen*.

**the** works the same way. Only *der* words change: **der** becomes **den**. *die*, *das* and the plural *die* stay the same.

- *Der Tisch ist neu.* (subject)
- *Ich brauche **den** Tisch.* (object)

grammarNotes.title: One pattern: den, einen, keinen, meinen
grammarNotes.body:
All the little words before a *der* noun change in the same way when the noun is the object: they end in **-en**.

*dein, sein, ihr* and *Ihr* follow *mein*: *Ich finde **deinen** Balkon schön.*

*die* and *das* words never change in the accusative, so you only have to watch out for *der* words.

grammarNotes.title: Describing things: sein and finden
grammarNotes.body:
After **sein** (to be) and **finden** (to find, to think), an adjective has **no ending**. It just goes at the end:

- *Die Küche ist **groß**.*
- *Ich finde die Wohnung **gemütlich**.* (I think the flat is cosy.)

To ask what something is like: **Wie ist …?** To ask someone's opinion: **Wie findest du …?** or **Wie finden Sie …?** *finden* adds an *e* in *du findest* and *er findet*, like *arbeiten*.

Make an adjective stronger or weaker:

- **sehr** = very: *sehr hell*
- **zu** = too, which means it's a problem: *zu klein*
- **nicht so** = not very: *nicht so laut*

grammarNotes.title: Viewing a flat
grammarNotes.body:
Use **Sie** with a landlord (*der Vermieter*) or landlady (*die Vermieterin*).

Rents are in hundreds. Say the number, then **hundert**, all as one word: *acht + hundert = **achthundert***. *Euro* has no plural: *achthundert Euro*.

Flat sizes are in **Quadratmeter** (square metres): *sechzig Quadratmeter* = 60 m².
table: Ich finde die Küche sehr schön.
say you want to rent it

exercises.title: Die Wohnung
exercises.body:
**die Wohnung** is a flat or apartment. You know the verb *wohnen* (to live), and *Wohnung* comes from it.

**das Zimmer** is a room. Put another word in front to say which room:

- *schlafen* (to sleep) + *Zimmer* = **das Schlafzimmer**, the bedroom
- *wohnen* (to live) + *Zimmer* = **das Wohnzimmer**, the living room

The last part decides the article, so both are *das*.

exercises.instruction: der, die or das? Think of Zimmer.

exercises.title: Balkon and Garten
exercises.body:
- **der Balkon** = the balcony. Stress the end: *bal-KOHN*.
- **der Garten** = the garden. Plural: *die Gärten*.

To show someone around, say **Das ist …** To ask where a room is: **Wo ist …?**

examples.translation: The garden is there on the left.

exercises.translation: This is the kitchen.

exercises.title: Die Wohnung hat …
exercises.body:
To say what a flat has, use **haben**. The rooms are the object, so *der* words take **einen**, just like *Ich habe einen Bruder*:

- *Die Wohnung hat **einen** Balkon.*
- *Die Wohnung hat **eine** Küche und **ein** Bad.*

You can also use **es gibt**: *Es gibt einen Garten.*

*Zimmer* is the same in the plural: *drei Zimmer*.

exercises.translation: The flat has a balcony.
exercises.hint: a, der word as the object

exercises.translation: The flat has two rooms and a kitchen.
exercises.answer: Die Wohnung hat zwei Zimmer und eine Küche.

exercises.translation: The house has a garden.

exercises.text: Die Wohnung hat drei Zimmer, eine Küche und ein Bad.
exercises.translation: The flat has three rooms, a kitchen and a bathroom.
exercises.hint: Wohnung: a long o, VOH-noong. Zimmer starts with a ts sound.

exercises.title: Furniture
exercises.body:
Learn each word with its article. Tap to hear them.

*st* at the start of a word sounds like *sht*: **Stuhl** is *shtool*.

Some plurals add an umlaut: *der Stuhl → die Stühle*, *der Schrank → die Schränke*.

exercises.title: brauchen: to need
exercises.body:
**brauchen** = to need. It's regular:

- ich brauche
- du brauchst
- er / sie braucht
- wir / sie / Sie brauchen

The thing you need is the object, so *der* words take **einen**, just like after *möchten* and *haben*.

exercises.translation: I need a cupboard.
exercises.hint: a, der word as the object

exercises.title: der becomes den
exercises.body:
*ein* becomes *einen* for an object. **the** does the same: **der** becomes **den**.

- *Der Tisch ist hier.* The table is here. (subject)
- *Ich brauche **den** Tisch.* I need the table. (object)

Only *der* words change. *die*, *das* and the plural *die* stay the same.

exercises.instruction: Which form fits? Ich brauche ___ Stuhl.
Which form fits? Brauchst du ___ Sofa?

exercises.translation: We don't need the table.
exercises.hint: the, der word as the object

exercises.source: Ich brauche ein Bett und einen Schrank.
accepted: I need a bed and a cupboard.
I need a bed and a wardrobe.

exercises.text: Ich brauche einen Tisch und zwei Stühle.
exercises.translation: I need a table and two chairs.
exercises.hint: Stühle: the st sounds like sht, and the ü is long.

exercises.title: Die Küche ist groß.
exercises.body:
To describe something, use **sein** + an adjective. The adjective goes at the end and **never changes**, whether the noun is *der*, *die* or *das*.

Adjectives are easy to learn in opposite pairs. You already know *alt* (old) from talking about age.

exercises.translation: The bathroom is small.

exercises.title: Wie ist …?
exercises.body:
To ask what something is like, say **Wie ist …?** (literally *How is …?*).

To ask about size, put the adjective after *wie*: **Wie groß ist …?** = How big is …?

examples.text: Die Küche ist groß und hell.
examples.translation: The kitchen is big and bright.

exercises.translation: The kitchen is big and bright.
exercises.answer: Die Küche ist groß und hell.

exercises.title: sehr, zu, nicht so
exercises.body:
Three little words change how strong an adjective is:

- **sehr** = very: *sehr hell*
- **zu** = too: *zu klein*. Like in English, *too* means it's a problem.
- **nicht so** = not very, not that: *nicht so groß*

*Das Zimmer ist sehr klein* is just a fact. *Das Zimmer ist **zu** klein* means it's too small for you.

examples.text: Das Bad ist nicht so groß.

exercises.instruction: The room is small, and that's a problem for you. What do you say?
options: Das Zimmer ist nicht so klein.

exercises.translation: The sofa is too old.

The table is new but the chair is old.
The table's new, but the chair's old.
The table's new but the chair's old.

exercises.translation: The bedroom is very dark.
How big is the kitchen?
exercises.hint: groß: a long o, like grohs. Küche: a short ü, then a soft ch.

exercises.title: Ich finde … schön.
exercises.body:
**finden** = to find. Germans also use it to give an opinion: *Ich finde die Wohnung schön.* = I think the flat is nice.

Like *arbeiten*, it adds an *e* in two forms:

- ich finde
- du **findest**
- er / sie **findet**
- wir / sie / Sie finden

To ask someone's opinion: **Wie findest du …?** or, politely, **Wie finden Sie …?**

examples.translation: I think the flat is beautiful.
What do you think of the sofa?

examples.text: Sie findet die Küche zu klein.
examples.translation: She thinks the kitchen is too small.

exercises.translation: What do you think of the room?
exercises.hint: finden → du … (add an e, like arbeitest)

exercises.title: gemütlich, ruhig, laut
exercises.body:
- **gemütlich** = cosy. A very German word: warm, comfortable and relaxed. You'll hear it a lot!
- **ruhig** = quiet, calm
- **laut** = loud, noisy

A short answer is fine too: *Wie findest du das Sofa? **Sehr gemütlich!***

mouthShapes.label: ü
mouthShapes.caption: gemütlich: say ee, then round your lips

examples.translation: The living room is very cosy.

exercises.title: Ich finde den Balkon schön.
exercises.body:
With *finden*, the thing you give an opinion on is the **object**. So *der* words take **den**:

- *Der Balkon ist schön.*
- *Ich finde **den** Balkon schön.*

*die* and *das* words don't change: *Ich finde **das** Bett gemütlich.*

The adjective goes at the very end, with no ending.

examples.translation: I think the balcony is beautiful.
What do you think of the garden?
I think the bed is comfortable.

exercises.translation: I think the sofa is very cosy.

exercises.title: One pattern for der words
exercises.body:
Now you've seen it four times. When a *der* word is the object, the word in front of it ends in **-en**:

- der → **den**
- ein → **einen**
- kein → **keinen**
- mein → **meinen** (and *deinen, seinen, ihren*)

*die* and *das* words never change in the accusative.

exercises.instruction: Which form fits? Wir haben ___ Garten.

exercises.translation: What do you think of my balcony?
exercises.hint: my, der word as the object

exercises.translation: What do you think of the living room? Very cosy!

exercises.title: Flat hunting
exercises.body:
- **die Miete** = the rent
- **der Vermieter / die Vermieterin** = the landlord / the landlady. Both contain *Miete*!
- **Wie hoch ist die Miete?** = How much is the rent? Learn it as a fixed phrase.
- **der Quadratmeter** = square metre: *sechzig Quadratmeter* = 60 m²
- **mieten** = to rent: *Ich möchte die Wohnung mieten.*

Rents are in hundreds: *acht + hundert = **achthundert***, written as one word.

Use **Sie** with a landlord.

examples.translation: The flat is sixty square metres.
I'd like to rent the flat.
